input: I take the tea and sit where everyone can hear without having to gather around me. "Three short pages. The courier has excellent reasons for everything." I read the story aloud: a courier reaches a bridge whose keeper asks a penny. He decides the stream is narrow enough to jump. He leaves his boots on the bank to keep them dry, jumps, and discovers halfway across that he has measured the distance from the wrong stone. He loses the parcel in the water. While he retrieves it, a goat carries off one boot and the current takes the other. The keeper helps him out and offers him a seat. The courier spends the walk home explaining that his mistake was taking too little of a run-up. I finish with the keeper hanging the penny toll sign a little higher, out of the goat's reach, and put my pages down. I leave the room space to react without apologizing for the story first.
output:
For the first page, the only interruption is porcelain settling onto saucers. At the wrong stone, Ysolde’s gaze sharpens. When the goat takes the first boot, Rashid gives one startled bark of laughter and covers it with his hand.

“Do not encourage the goat,” Caelindra murmurs, though her ears have tilted forward and her mouth is betraying her.

The last line lands. A brief silence follows—not polite, but occupied by the sign, the goat, and one barefoot man still explaining himself down the road.

Ashara’s tail knocks once against her chair. “He should have paid the penny.”

“Then there would be no story,” Rashid says.

“He would still have boots.”

“That is rarely the chief concern of literature.”

Thessaly releases her string bridge. It vanishes between her fingers. “I wanted the keeper to receive his penny. I know there is no penny. I wanted it anyway.”

Seraphel raises her cup.

“The goat showed sense, the man showed none;  
I mourn each boot, but liked the fun.”

“He does not improve,” Ysolde says. “That was wise. Three pages are insufficient to repair some people.”

Rashid leans back, grinning. “Nahla would demand a sequel from the goat’s perspective.”

Caelindra has not joined the argument. She extends one pale-gold hand toward your pages, stopping short of touching them.

“The final image is your strongest,” she says. “There is one explanation immediately before it that may blunt the ending. I could show you where.” Her tone grows markedly more formal. “If criticism was included in the invitation. If not, I have merely enjoyed it and consumed your tea.”

Across the room, the clock’s long hand creeps toward sixth bell. Ashara glances at Caelindra, then at you, plainly awaiting the ruling.
